title: Avoid Illusions of Knowing
coreMove: Make confidence answer to a cue-free check before treating it as knowledge.
sourcePressure: The chapter focuses on calibration: familiarity, rereading, and fluent recognition inflate confidence unless learners use tests, explanations, delayed recall, and external feedback.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer must avoid making confidence the enemy; the problem is untested confidence that borrows support from visible cues.

sourceAnchors.name: Catherine Johnson
sourceAnchors.detail: Minneapolis Police Department lieutenant describing simulations, including a traffic stop where a trunk popped open and a shotgun appeared, and a gun-disarming routine that once trained an officer to hand the gun back.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Catherine Johnson’s officers learned that practice can teach exactly the wrong automatic move if nobody checks what the drill is really installing.

sourceAnchors.name: Loftus car-crash wording study
sourceAnchors.detail: People estimated a higher speed when asked how fast cars were going when they smashed into each other than when asked when they contacted each other.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: One verb can tilt memory enough to make certainty feel cleaner than it deserves.

sourceAnchors.name: China Airlines spatial-disorientation incident
sourceAnchors.detail: The index and notes place the China Airlines incident in the chapter as an example of trained judgment being hijacked by a wrong mental model.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A cockpit can punish certainty that has not been checked against the instruments.

hook: Do not open by saying learning is harder than it looks
Do not use a generic desk-and-notes image
Do not start with a broad claim about students today
counterintuition: Do not use the shell easier is not better
Do not flatten the chapter into struggle is good
Do not contrast comfort and growth in generic coaching language
tryThisNow: Do not write set a timer and reflect
Do not ask for a vague study audit
Do not use a reusable close-your-notes prompt without a chapter-specific action
examples: No repeated mug, marker, dosing cup, bike helmet, radiator, bus depot, classroom, or narrow-kitchen shells
No six examples that all start with a timestamp and a named protagonist
No generic student rereads notes scene unless the visible beat changes the method

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective reveal, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.domain: Grace, a radiology resident reviewing chest films
exampleSpecs.audience: advanced learners who feel sure because a pattern looks familiar
exampleSpecs.stakes: an overconfident first read could miss a subtle pneumothorax
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she writes the diagnosis, then covers it and forces herself to name the disconfirming signs before checking the attending note
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A pale crescent hides near the top of the lung field.

exampleSpecs.domain: Ben, a climber checking knot knowledge after months off
exampleSpecs.audience: hobbyists who mistake recognition of a knot diagram for competence
exampleSpecs.stakes: a partner will trust the knot on a real route
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he ties the knot without the guide, stress-tests it, finds the wrong tail length, and reties before leaving the gym floor
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 7:48 p.m., Ben pulls the rope through his harness in silence.

exampleSpecs.domain: Margaux, a tax preparer auditing new deduction rules
exampleSpecs.audience: professionals who remember where the rule sits on a page but not what it means
exampleSpecs.stakes: a client return could be filed on borrowed certainty
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: her senior asks her to explain the rule for a changed client case before she can search the PDF
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "Explain it without the PDF," the senior says.

exampleSpecs.domain: Lars, a flight-sim trainee after a smooth autopilot lesson
exampleSpecs.audience: trainees whose confidence comes from ideal conditions
exampleSpecs.stakes: instrument failure will reveal whether the procedure is independent
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the instructor blanks one display and asks Lars to state the cross-check before touching the controls

exampleSpecs.domain: Paula, a museum conservator identifying varnish damage
exampleSpecs.audience: specialists who trust the first familiar label
exampleSpecs.stakes: wrong treatment can damage the painting surface
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the postmortem shows how a delayed peer check caught that her confident identification came from one familiar stain pattern
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Paula a second lamp angle to lose her certainty.

exampleSpecs.domain: Hadiya, a policy analyst preparing briefing numbers
exampleSpecs.audience: knowledge workers who feel numbers are learned because the spreadsheet is open
exampleSpecs.stakes: a minister may ask for the logic behind the figures without the file
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: you watch her close the sheet, reconstruct the three assumptions, then reopen it to find which one was only recognition
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You see the spreadsheet vanish and the room get quieter.

skillTargets: choose cue-free checks that expose borrowed confidence
interpret fluency as a weak calibration signal
use feedback without turning every hesitation into failure

tryThisNowSpec: Before rereading a marked page, close it and explain the point in three sentences; then reopen it and mark only what your explanation missed.

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
